u_\ell$ with 10.7 fb$^{-1}$, in addition to differential cross-sections and $\dfrac{d^2\Gamma}{dp_\perp^2dp_\parallel}$ distributions. Our findings are in line with existing predictions.

In recent years, the combination of sophisticated spectroscopy and advanced computing has led to a significant expansion of the exoplanet exodus. The cross-correlation technique, which compares the light of exoplanets to a database of stellar atmospheres, has become a key method in this progression. However, traditional methods for separating exoplanetary light from starlight have limitations, particularly at high signal-to-noise ratios. To overcome this challenge, the Light Field Spectrometer, a new class of photonic devices utilizing waveguides and leaky resonators, offers a promising solution. By replacing conventional gratings with these photonic elements, the Light Field Spectrometer can achieve a broader spectral range and higher efficiency. The novel photonic technology has the potential to increase the yield of exoplanet discoveries and advance the field of exoplanetary exploration.

In recent years, various deep learning approaches have emerged to tackle the similarity assessment and ranking tasks within pairwise drug comparison. This paper examines and compares the performance of a broad range of deep learning models. Our analysis reveals that graph-based models outperform other alternatives, but also highlights that when graph models incorporate drug component descriptions, they achieve superior drug similarity estimation. Furthermore, we validate that edge-based drug similarity metrics produced by graph models can be effectively utilized in two-link prediction tasks: identifying bridging compounds between distinct disease treatment categories and identifying potential follow-up medications.

A critical aspect of maintaining transportation networks is identifying potential issues in roads. This process has been complicated by factors such as the cost of manual inspections and limited availability of trained personnel. Fortunately, advancements in computer vision technology have enabled more efficient and cost-effective automated inspections. This research presents a novel approach to identifying road problems using a diverse dataset of images from multiple countries, which was created by combining existing image collections. By pre-training models on this aggregated dataset and fine-tuning them individually for each country, the study achieved outstanding results, surpassing the accuracy of models trained on the full dataset. Notably, the proposed models demonstrated exceptional performance across various road conditions and exhibited strong generalizability.

Imitation learning allows a robot to learn tasks by watching humans or other robots, even without explicit explanations. The challenge lies in capturing subtle task-related human behaviors from visual data alone. To overcome this, our approach uses two distinct camera perspectives to better represent tasks. By having the robot observe humans from the same relative viewpoint as the instructional videos, our method effectively translates visual cues into actionable information. This approach falls under the umbrella of cross-domain imitation learning, as it bridges the gap between the taught and the robot's environment. Our framework combines this perspective alignment with a cycle-consistent adversarial network to translate visual information into control instructions. As a result, our model outperforms existing single-domain methods and achieves remarkable results on complex 3D manipulation tasks.

A numerical investigation into the role of magnetic fields in disk formation around Population III protostars reveals significant amplification of these fields through rapid rotation, eliminating fragmentation even at low densities. We discovered that magnetic field growth is greatly amplified in Population III stars due to their high rotation rates, and this growth is primarily facilitated by the tension of magnetic field lines wrapping around the protostar and stretched in the axial direction, rather than by expansion or shear effects. As a result, we found that in many cases, magnetic field growth is exponentially amplified, leading to a complete elimination of disk fragmentation. Specifically, fields initially at a strength of 10^-3 Gauss are quickly amplified to 100 Gauss, and this amplification occurs on a timescale comparable to the orbital period of the orbit in question. Moreover, we observed that this rapid magnetic field growth effectively eliminates a wide range of previously identified fragmentation-free parameters, and this effect is largely independent of the initial magnetic field strength and strength ratios.

Recent research has focused on identifying a minimal subset of data-driven association rules, with the goal of recovering key insights without being overwhelmed by irrelevant findings. Two main approaches have been taken: one involves selecting a few meaningful rules, and the other involves deducing important conclusions from a reduced set. This work unifies these lines of research, providing a framework for both reducing data redundancy and making inferences, based on a newly discovered relationship between the redundancy-based minimum subset and concepts from closed itemset mining.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently experience mental health challenges.  A key issue arises from the intersection of criminal justice and mental health, specifically regarding the balance between public safety and the rights of individuals.  While the criminal justice system prioritizes accountability and punishment, the mental health system focuses on rehabilitation.  In an effort to combine the strengths of both systems, many criminal justice jurisdictions now provide mental health treatment to individuals who have been convicted of a crime.  This paper examines the impact of a mental health treatment program on individuals within the criminal justice system in Florida, which offers therapy to prisoners and inmates who have been sentenced to less than two years in prison.  Our analysis utilizes administrative data from the state of Florida and compares it to individual arrest records.  We find that access to this mental health treatment program has a significant positive impact on individuals' outcomes, specifically reducing their likelihood of being re-arrested and also decreasing the severity of subsequent arrests.  These benefits are observed even when controlling for a wide range of factors and are more pronounced among individuals who have been arrested for violent crimes.  Moreover, we find that the positive effects of this mental health treatment program are more evident among individuals who have been convicted of crimes and are therefore more likely to participate in the program, as opposed to those who have not been convicted and are therefore less likely to participate in the program.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach for creating a comprehensive, real-time, and dynamic representation of the wireless environment. This type of mapping system can provide detailed information about the coverage area, including the connection quality and location of wireless terminals. Currently, the process of gathering the data required to create a radio map is largely manual and labor-intensive, involving the use of drones or vehicles operated by humans. However, using autonomous drones to collect this data presents a more efficient and scalable solution. Although the idea of using drones to create radio maps is still in its infancy, several key challenges remain, including the limitations of current drones, the need for real-time data analysis, and the development of efficient data collection strategies. This paper delves into the theoretical aspects and practical applications of using drones to create radio maps, exploring cutting-edge techniques and approaches to overcome the identified challenges.

This paper outlines a novel approach for identifying unusual patterns in time-series data using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Additional Gauge Likelihood Assessments (ALAs). The ALA complements the traditional observation likelihood assessment (OLA) by focusing on features outside the primary model's correlations. Since HMMs cannot accurately predict data with strong trends or recurring patterns, additional gauge metrics are employed to detect and quantify such characteristics. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated using synthetic data, comparing it to a competing model-based technique.

This research proposes a multi-sensory person authentication system that integrates the results of thermal, visual, and auditory modalities. Individually, these sensors can be used for person verification, but combining them improves resilience against environmental interference and evasion. In this study, we compared the resilience of unimodal and combined modalities against various attacks, including fake identities and altered environment conditions. Our findings show that a multi-sensory authentication system outperforms single-modality approaches in evasion resistance. Our study's outcomes contribute to the development of more reliable and secure biometric systems.

We created a framework to increase the size of training datasets for neural network models, allowing for improved generalization. When starting with an existing labeled dataset, we can create new examples by altering the labeling process simulating different sources of noise. Our method simulates this variability by applying random perturbations to inputs and comparing the altered output with the original, creating examples that a neural network needs to handle. We tested this approach on two tasks: machine translation and automatic speech recognition. In both cases, our technique significantly boosted the accuracy of the models and even outperformed a model trained on a larger dataset.

Research has been conducted to estimate a distribution or a parameter derived from a mixture of distributions, and the focus is on a finite mixture of exponential families with a parameterized mixing distribution, and a finite mixture with known distributions but unknown parameters. We propose two generalized estimation methods for the mean of the mixing distribution, and the first method involves estimating the parameters of the component distributions using maximum likelihood estimation and then applying smoothed estimation. The second method involves directly estimating the density function of the mixture and then using smoothed estimation to estimate the mean of the mixing distribution. Both methods have been tested in simulations and show that the second method generally outperform the first. We have also provided real data applications for the described methods and these include the analysis of a dataset of discrete lifetimes of devices, the examination of device failure times from two separate tests, and the examination of device failure times.

Achieving a balance between data protection and utility in big data analytics is a pressing issue. To address this, a new concept known as one-sided differential privacy has been developed, which allows for one party to share their private information securely without compromising another party's utility. However, existing frameworks assume that data from different sources is independent, which is not always the case in real-world scenarios. When attributes within a dataset are interrelated, there's a risk that one-sided differential privacy fails to protect the remaining attributes. This paper identifies such vulnerabilities, which were previously overlooked, and proposes an enhanced model to mitigate them. The proposed model ensures robust protection for all attributes and achieves optimal information transmission between parties. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated through numerical examples.

The presence of gas and dust gaps in protoplanetary disks is likely a result of planet formation processes. A case study of the AS 209 disk, which exhibits coexisting millimeter and submillimeter gaps, was analyzed using ALMA data. This research found that the thermal structure derived from continuum observations is inconsistent with dust settling due to planet formation, suggesting that non-thermal emission processes are responsible for the observed emission profile. Multiple emission models were tested and found that grain growth and electrostatic charging could not reproduce the observed data. As a result, two processes that could create the emission profile were identified: (1) carbon monoxide depletion by factors of 2-5 from the gas phase, and (2) emission suppression at larger radii due to a higher degree of CO depletion in the dense disk midplane. These findings suggest a complex interaction between gas and dust in the AS 209 disk, and the need for further research to determine the role of planet formation in shaping co-existing gaps.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, yet the necessary tools for this analysis are underdeveloped. Existing solutions are either too limited in scope or have specific functions scattered across different platforms, resulting in a lack of comprehensive toolkits. This study is addressing this issue by presenting a C++-based software framework, timeb, designed for the precise analysis of time-stamped measurements. With a user-friendly interface and extensive toolset, timeb offers a range of features, including visualizations, flexible tool integration, and easy-to-use programming interfaces, making it a perfect fit for both interactive exploration and automated processing of time-stamped data.

The objective of this study is to demonstrate the presence of'mild solutions' for a first-order mean field game involving controls with linear state constraints that derive from a vector field. These games can be thought of as the probabilistic formulation of mean field games with constraints on the amount of resource distribution. Due to the restrictive constraints, solution regularity is compromised, leading to solutions with solutions that are continuous but only weakly so. This research also includes specific examples illustrating the potential for no solution or non-unique solution in certain scenarios.

Recent research has highlighted the significance of the Galactic stellar distribution in the sub-parsec scale. A novel method is introduced here to identify and study the one-dimensional stellar structures, or "strings," within this framework. These structures are defined by excesses of point sources along linear features. We utilize the Gaia DR2 catalog, focusing on stars within the central 300 parsecs of the Galaxy. Our approach involves using the Gaia DR2 data to uncover these structures, with a focus on the Southern Hemisphere. We identify approximately 20 such strings within the inner 100 parsecs of the Galaxy. Our analysis suggests that many of these structures are composed of moving groups and clusters, rather than random alignments. However, it is also possible that some of these structures are formed through line-of-sight effects, such as those caused by the spiral arms. Our findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the nature of these structures and their potential implications for the study of the Galaxy.

For retail establishments, ensuring visual harmony between garments is a complex task.
We introduce VICTOR, an advanced system that identifies pairs of articles of clothing which do not style well together.
Our method leverages pre-trained fashion contrastive models, fine-tuned on a comprehensive dataset of 20,000 uniquely designed outfits.
The inherent ability of these models to capture subtle aesthetic principles enables effective detection of non-compatible clothing combinations.
Evaluations demonstrate the superior performance of our fashion contrastive pre-training over both generic image-text models and a model trained from scratch on clothing data, particularly in handling abstract aesthetic concepts.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced our understanding of classical and quantum systems. Nonetheless, its application to the characterization of novel forms of optical nonclassicality is in its infancy. Through a straightforward analytical method, we can examine the optical system's state space, identifying distinct regions where specific nonclassical traits emerge. The proposed method enables the proposal of new resource theories, with corresponding monotones that quantify the concentration of quantum characteristics. The optimal coherence cost is utilized to introduce a novel monotone, allowing for a comparison with the concentration of pure quantum states. The developed approach is exemplified by the examination of qubit systems.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly slow down the overall process. The FBA protocol was introduced to tackle this issue by enabling asynchronous communication between the client and server. Building on previous research where FBA was found stable under specific conditions, this paper delves into the behavior of L\'evy flights--extremely long exploration patterns--in asynchronous federated learning environments. Specifically, this work investigates how updates made by devices with slow latencies can lead to unbounded flights, causing devices to consistently send updates.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping theoretical underpinnings within polynomial tempered distribution space, along with related (ultra)distributions. Ultimately, we demonstrate that this calculus yields representations of operator functions within pertinent function spaces.

Recent research suggests that the value of the scalar field's slope in the Einstein frame is restricted, which in turn limits the maximum reheater temperature in the early universe. This limitation results in reducing the population of dark matter in the form of initial black holes to less than 0.1 percent.

We examine the dynamics of one phase in a material undergoing a phase transition using a model that represents different components as particles. Specifically, we focus on the phase transition between a gaseous and a solid state. Our analysis reveals that the boundaries between these phases are characterized by distinct structures, or rifts, which take the form of rafts. These solid structures float within the gaseous phase and have internal compositions that are analogous to Landau's model for superfluid helium. Additionally, we identify that the boundaries themselves can exhibit internal structures, or rifts, which are caused by variations in the orientation of the solid phases. These variations result in the formation of grain boundaries that resemble the crystalline structures of polycrystals. Furthermore, we observe that the boundary between the phases is composed of a mixture of different-sized polycrystalline structures, ranging from small grains to larger, more ordered regions. These findings provide a new perspective on the dynamics of phase transitions and the resulting structures.

The main issue hindering the widespread use of gallium nitride (GaN) in high-frequency and power electronic devices is its nearly zero thermal conductivity, which is 10 times lower than silicon. Researchers have been exploring methods to enhance the thermal properties of GaN, such as introducing nanostructures or defects, but these approaches have not been successfully implemented in the source region of transistors. A new method has been developed to improve the thermal conductivity of GaN by carefully matching its lattice structure with other materials. By matching the anisotropic strain between GaN and a thin film of zinc germanium nitride or magnesium silicon nitride, researchers have been able to expand the GaN's bandgap without incurring additional strain. This results in a 20% increase in the electron mobility, which translates to a 20% increase in the transconductance. A simulation using the drift-diffusion model confirms that the GaN channel's performance is improved when its lattice structure is expanded through matching with these materials.

One key issue in mobile robotics is path planning, which is often achieved through navigation techniques such as Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). However, incorporating time information into GPR can lead to over-fitting due to an excessive number of data points. To address this limitation, our research introduces a novel approach, known as Exponential Covariance Plus Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (EC-KRH) learning. By combining the principles of Gaussian Process Temporal Difference (GP-TD) learning and sparse approximation, our method allows for efficient online learning of a value function, which is then used to determine the optimal action at each step of the navigation process. The experimental findings demonstrate that our proposed technique outperforms several existing methods, including Gaussian Process Temporal Difference (GP-TD), in terms of training speed, generalization, and the ability to avoid over-fitting.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a conformal Gauss map of constant mean curvature, identifying two key transformations that preserve this property. The surface in question can be expressed as the sum of two minimal surfaces, and this relationship is utilized to establish the transformations. The new surfaces created through these transformations share the same conformal Gauss map, and we investigate their properties in relation to this common attribute.

We develop a direct method for approximating nonparametric conditional expectation operators, analyzing both the speed of approximation and convergence rates for the resulting operators. This approach leads to new inequalities that can facilitate the approximation of other types of operators. Utilizing this technique, we can efficiently approximate powers of a transfer operator, a stochastic evolution operator, and high-dimensional conditional expectation operators. In doing so, we also address the problems of statistical estimation for a transition probability measure and the computation of a conditional expectation.

This paper builds upon recent research by Kim et. al. by examining a specific variation of r-stirling numbers with a parameter λ, denoted as Sλ(n,k), and defines an associated polynomial. With this foundation, we identify a relationship between these unusual stirling numbers and certain coefficients, ultimately yielding a connection to λ-binomials. We then derive and verify a corresponding identity.

Despite significant advancements, it's still challenging to build dynamic models that outperform static models on various tasks, particularly when it comes to predicting future relationships in temporal knowledge graphs. Our research investigates why static models can perform better and demonstrates that they have not been fully exploited in previous studies. We found that many claimed improvements over static models are actually due to experimental errors, such as using different static and dynamic models for baseline comparisons and including unnecessary temporal features. As a result, we have developed the first ever temporal knowledge graph benchmark, which allows for fair comparisons and the effective use of static models. Our benchmark reveals that, on average, static models perform just 0.2% worse than dynamic models, indicating that the latter do offer some benefits. Based on these findings, we have created a set of guidelines to help future studies in the field. Our benchmark and accompanying recommendations are available at https://github.com/TKGBench/TKGBench.

This note examines relationships between directed graphs and the C*-algebras associated with them, specifically focusing on strong shift equivalence. We establish that strong shift equivalence between finite directed graphs implies strong Morita equivalence of their associated C*-algebras. Additionally, we examine whether this implication holds for infinite graphs, but find that it does not always be the case. We also explore conditions under which it does hold, providing examples to illustrate instances where it fails.

In this study, we examine the complex tomographic structure of gluon-glyphon-gluon bound states at a non-zero magnetic field in QCD, considering both parallel and perpendicular directions relative to the field. Our analysis is grounded in a novel approach that incorporates multiple color channels and generalized propagator structures for heavy quark pairs. We calculate distinct helicity bound states in a quenched QCD with an anisotropic UV cutoff, demonstrating that magnetic fields significantly impact these bound states by altering their dissociation patterns. Our findings are visually represented through tomographic images of gluon-glyphon-gluon bound states, highlighting their directional dependencies and providing a deeper understanding of quark confinement influenced by external magnetic fields.

Recent advances in pre-trained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, including the challenging task of answering questions. Building on their success, researchers have explored incorporating graph neural networks and attention mechanisms to improve question-answering performance. Our work builds on these findings, and also draws inspiration from symbolic reasoning, by introducing KBRoLE, a novel hybrid model that combines knowledge base learning and pre-trained language models for improved question-answering. Specifically, our approach uses KBRoLE to perform role-based logical inference on entity pairs from knowledge graphs, enabling the identification of suitable answers that can then be fine-tuned by a pre-trained language model. Evaluations on two question-answering benchmarks demonstrate that the integration of knowledge graph reasoning significantly boosts model performance.

We have developed a novel method for constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon the pioneering work of Gopan, Kulkarni, and Mader, our approach generalizes their findings, which specifically involved finite group actions. By applying this general construction to examples of hyperbolic posets and flag complexes derived from group posets, we are able to produce new, previously unknown infinite families of high dimensional expanders.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language descriptions, yet the effectiveness of such descriptions heavily relies on the creativity of human input. In an effort to diversify these descriptions and enhance their range, a method has been proposed that leverages GPT-3's capability to generate a multitude of unique descriptions for tasks not included in its training data. By fine-tuning the model on prompt templates utilizing task information from benchmarks, it can produce a variety of descriptions that can be tested across different datasets. This approach is demonstrated to yield descriptions that, despite being similar in quality to those provided by humans, offer a notable improvement over those provided without fine-tuning and can also be used to create descriptions for tasks that are already present in the benchmark. Furthermore, the analysis of the model's performance across multiple datasets has shed light on the sources of variation in zero-shot performance, ultimately leading to a greater understanding of the potential and limitations of creative prompt engineering.

We've established a criterion to determine when the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space of global $\mathbb{Q}$-invariants in the completed Hecke algebra is non-empty for a weight one Hilbert-Siegel modular form of a specific type. By combining this result with earlier work by Cornut-Vatanelis, we've drawn conclusions about the existence of global $\mathbb{Q}$-invariants in the associated Helleseth-Ingram algebra. Furthermore, we've computed and published the rational eigenvalues, along with their multiplicities, for the spaces of Hilbert-Siegel modular forms, both with and without characters, defined over quadratic fields and related to Artin motives.

Detecting and differentiating between multiple microwave signals is crucial in microwave communication and electron spin resonance systems. However, traditional methods struggle with accurately identifying unknown frequencies, modulations, and amplitude variations. A novel approach leverages Rydberg atoms' sensitive response to electric fields, combined with multifrequency measurement, to capture a comprehensive Rydberg atom spectrum enhanced by deep learning. This approach allows for extracting and analyzing the original microwave signals from the captured spectrum. Simulations demonstrate a 90% accuracy in frequency identification, while also revealing enhanced features of modulation parameters that traditional methods fail to reveal.

We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the spiral galaxy UGC 8839, focusing on its inner region. By creating a detailed velocity field from 2D HI and CO observations, we determined that the inner parts of the galaxy exhibit low non-circular motions. This allowed us to create an accurate rotation curve that is flat at a level of approximately 78 km/s out to a radius of 6.5 kpc. This is the farthest such measurement for an HI rotation curve. Additionally, our analysis of the rotation curve's shape and its constancy over a large range of radii, combined with a thorough examination of the mass distribution, led us to determine that the mass-to-light ratio is constant at a value of 0.54 solar masses per luminosity. This is the first time such a ratio has been determined in such detail. Our analysis also revealed that the outer parts of the HI disk are warped, with a maximum tilt of approximately 10 degrees, and our current understanding of this warping is that it is a result of a constant rate of angular momentum loss.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under certain conditions.

The primary source of atmospheric heating on Earth's upper layers is the interaction of gravity waves with small-scale wind layers, a phenomenon also observed on Mars. This process is a significant factor in the complex dynamics of the Martian atmosphere, as evidenced by the coupling of its electrodynamic and gravito-buoyant components in its middle and upper regions, respectively. This interaction is particularly evident in the coupling of gravity waves in the Martian atmosphere, as evidenced by the presence of meso-scale temperature and density variations in the space between its upper and surface layers. This study aims to provide a comprehensive review of gravity waves on Mars, focusing on their characteristics, distribution, and propagation, based on the observations made by the Mars Global Surveyor, Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and the Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution Mission orbiters, which have facilitated the identification and analysis of such waves through the measurement of thermal infrared data.

The LHC has achieved record-breaking energies and luminosity in its proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions, allowing for remarkable photon-photon interactions at very high energies. These interactions can be harnessed to produce various final states, including charmonium particles like the J/ψ meson, which can be used to probe QCD in extreme conditions. Recent findings from ALICE on energy loss and production mechanisms of J/ψ in lead-lead collisions, as well as measurements of forward J/ψ production in ultra-peripheral interactions, are discussed in this report.

Recent advancements in natural language processing and computer vision have
significantly benefited from the incorporation of deep learning, a key
component of which is the utilization of recurrent neural networks (RNNs). RNNs
are uniquely suited to handle sequential data, making them highly effective for
such applications. This paper delves into the fundamental principles behind RNNs
and their success in capturing temporal information, as well as an exploration
of their broader uses in computer vision and natural language processing.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a complex issue, with the relationship between economic impact and health consequences not straightforward. We investigate how early implementation of effective mitigation measures impacts this relationship, and our results show that taking significant measures quickly leads to a consistent pattern of economic loss decreasing as health damage does, across a wide range of scenarios. This insight is valuable for policymakers, as it implies that prioritizing public health can also yield substantial economic benefits.

This paper presents an innovative approach to examining machine learning pipelines that utilize data and model components, aiming to provide insights into their behavior, particularly in cases of unexpected machine output. We propose two primary metrics, the Shapley Importance of Data (SID) and the Model, to assess the relative significance of individual data samples and model components in altering the predictions made by the pipeline. Our experiments, conducted on synthetic and real-world data, show that these metrics successfully identify anomalous data points and model components that may be contributing to incorrect outputs. Additionally, we provide practical applications of these metrics in pipeline diagnosis, as demonstrated in cases involving the MNIST dataset and a neural model trained over it.

This work begins by introducing two distinct yet interconnected concepts in detail. First, we will discuss Macdonald polynomials and second, cohomological field theories, or CHTs. Each of these ideas opens up a vast realm for exploration, thus allowing for consideration within a single narrative. The motivation behind combining these concepts stems from observing that each individually possesses rich implications in multiple fields, yet their intersection has even more significant consequences. Specifically, we will demonstrate how Macdonald polynomials play a significant role in representation theory, algebraic combinatorics, statistical mechanics, and conformal field theory. Furthermore, CHTs can be utilized to describe phenomena in geometric engineering of BPS states within string theory and telescopic evaluations of Donkin polynomials.

This study brings to light the significance of lattice symmetry in triangular structures for producing the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn. An investigation of pressure's impact on Anomalous Hall Effect in Mn$_3$Sn reveals an initial pressure-induced decrease in AHE, followed by AHE suppression at higher pressure. A theoretical analysis suggests that pressure transforms Mn$_3$Sn from a helical antiferromagnet to a collinear antiferromagnet, effectively eliminating AHE. Furthermore, first-principles calculations indicate that AHE can be restored by applying external stress to the collinear antiferromagnetic state, B-type AHE, through interlayer coupling. This study provides a framework for exploring AHE in Mn$_3$Sn and related compounds, as well as for investigating the influence of lattice symmetry on electronic properties in Mn-based semimetals.

Relation extraction is a key natural language processing task that involves
identifying and structuring relationships between entities within text. This
task has significant applications in areas such as question answering,
semantic search, and knowledge graph completion. Despite being an essential
component of NLP, accurately extracting relations from complex and ambiguous
text remains a challenging task. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of
deep neural network methods for relation extraction, discussing various
approaches, including schema-governed and schema-agnostic techniques. We also
evaluate the effectiveness of different models, evaluate functions, and pair
representation methods through extensive experiments using publicly available
datasets.

This paper delves into a mixed Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the -laplacian in a particular class of domains featuring reflectional symmetry. The chosen geometry includes domains formed by a two-dimensional cross-section extruded into three dimensions. Under specific conditions, it's demonstrated that the first few eigenvalues correspond to a large multiplicity and we identify an essential subset of the spectrum, ultimately leading to the derivation of asymptotic formulae for the large order Steklov-Robin eigenvalues.

We are investigating a crucial aspect of clustering algorithms, specifically how they can be used to identify significant substructures within complex networks. Our focus is on applying supertree algorithms to recover underlying bipartite graph patterns from observed networks, using various network types such as co-authorship systems, food web interactions, and trade networks as real-world examples. These algorithms leverage either pre-existing clusters from similar networks or labeled nodes in the network being analyzed to guide the supertree clustering process, which we assess using a new error rate metric for supertrees. Our initial findings suggest that supertree-based clustering can effectively capture essential features of these networks, including their hierarchical and cyclic characteristics.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document crucial patient information, 
allowing clinicians to make informed decisions.  However, radiologists face a 
notable time constraint of 3 to 5 seconds per chest X-ray (CXR) examination, 
compromising the quality and detail of each report.  This limitation poses a 
challenge for CXR analysis, as the reports' brevity and lack of context can be 
difficult for downstream NLP models to interpret accurately.  This study proposes 
an innovative approach of annotating CXR images with information derived from 
CT scans to bridge the gap between X-ray and CT findings in radiology reports. 
By segmenting and labeling patient anatomy on 2D CT projections, the method 
enables the development of a dataset with high-quality annotations that reflect 
anatomical locations and disease processes.  This data can be used to train 
models that distinguish between false positives and negatives in report findings, 
as demonstrated by a comparison of model performance with and without the 
annotated images.  This work aims to bridge the gap between CT and X-ray 
imaging and paves the way for advanced CXR analysis.

Bill Thurston initially discovered that Euler classes of taut foliations are bounded. 
This limit is re-examined in the context of tight contact structures within 3-manifolds. 
It is found that the set of Euler classes for tight contact structures is finite when 
one considers structures that are equivalent to an overtwisted structure through 
monodromy modifications. However, it is also shown that this set is not limited in 
cases where the structure remains essentially non-overtwisted despite numerous changes.
